title: Photography direction for a restaurant group
metaTitle: Photography direction for a restaurant group
excerpt: Choose photographs that show the room and one dish. A logo animation is not a picture of dinner. The frames are part of the argument a guest uses tonight.
alt: An open notebook with the word Notes underlined, a fountain pen, and glasses on a wooden desk, a place where the shot list can be written before anyone picks up a camera.
caption: Notes before the shoot. Direction starts as a sentence, not a filter. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first photograph show?
faqs.answer: The room a guest will sit in, or one dish from the menu, with the restaurant named in the caption. Both should appear before any animation. A logo drawing itself does not tell anyone where dinner is.

faqs.question: How do we brief the photographer?
faqs.answer: Give them one sentence: this frame has to show the seats and the light a guest will actually get, and this frame has to show one dish as it is served. Ask for the street, the room, and the plate. Reject frames that could be any group with the same linen.

faqs.question: Can we use a film?
faqs.answer: Yes, after the room and the dish are already visible, muted, with a caption that names the restaurant. Do not make the film the front door. A guest on a phone will not wait through a title sequence to learn if you are open.

markdown:
Direct restaurant group website photography so the pictures show the room and one dish. A guest deciding where to go tonight will judge the frames before they read a manifesto. A logo animation fails that guest. The pictures are part of the argument, not a mood pasted under the headline.

Choose what the frame must prove, then shoot for that proof. The room they will sit in. One plate as it leaves the pass. The neighborhood, if the neighborhood is the decision. Light and grade come after the sentence.

## The room and one dish

Every lead image needs a job you can say aloud. Show the twenty-four seats and the distance between them. Show the counter if the counter is the point. Show one dish, named, from the restaurant you are featuring. If you cannot say the job, the image is decoration, however fine the steam looks.

Write the job before the shoot. A photographer can chase hands and fire and still miss the chair a guest needs to see. Direction is the sentence. The camera keeps it.

Put the restaurant name and the dish name in text beside the image, not burned into the file. A guest should not need a click to learn which door this is. If the group has several rooms, an unlabeled plate is a way to book the wrong kitchen.

Reject a logo animation as the opening. It delays the room. It teaches the team that the mark is the product. The product is dinner. The mark can sit in the header, still, and small.

Wabisabi, a public Hanabi project, is a reminder that pictures work when they are chosen for a point of view. A restaurant site has a stricter test. The point of view has to be a room someone can book and a dish someone can order. A beautiful object is not yet a table.

## What to refuse

Keep a refuse list next to the selects.

- A logo animation, a monogram on a napkin, or a title sequence before the room.
- A skyline, a rented dining room, or a dish that is not on a menu you serve.
- Frames cropped so tight that the phone loses the table.
- Duplicate plates that differ only by a garnish you will not send.
- Any image you cannot caption with the restaurant and the decision.

Someone will love the slow-motion pour. Ask whether a stranger can tell where to go from it. If not, it can live lower, or not on the site. Do not accept a social edit unchanged. Social sequence is often atmosphere. Your site sequence is room, dish, neighborhood, menu.

Stock food photography is an obvious miss. Guests feel it. If you do not have the frame yet, use a plain sentence and shoot this week. A gap is more honest than a rented tart.

## A brief for the next service shoot

One page is enough. The decision sentence. The rooms that matter. The hour guests actually arrive, not only the golden minute. What you will not shoot. Privacy for staff and for guests who did not agree to be the campaign. A face in the room needs a yes.

Ask for a contact sheet before a heavy grade. Select for the argument, then grade. If you grade first, you will keep frames because the color flatters a plate you do not need.

Agree crops for the phone. The dish has to be recognizable at a small width. The room has to keep its seats. A crop that only works on a studio monitor will fail the visit that books the table.

Write captions the day you select. Future you will not remember which leek was Holt Street. The caption is the argument surviving the shoot. Include the dish name you are willing to update when the menu changes. Captions are content, not a flattened poster.

## Sequence, alt text, and weight

On the homepage, one room and one dish beat a carousel of twelve. Carousels hide the second proof. A guest who does not swipe still needs to know which restaurant and what dinner looks like.

On a restaurant's page, follow the sentence. Street. Room. Dish. A detail that would change the booking, such as a counter versus a booth. Then stop. The menu link should be in that sequence, not after a film.

The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treats images as content. Alt text should say what is in the frame: the room, the dish, the restaurant. Do not stuff a slogan into the alt. Do not leave it empty. The caption can carry the decision. The alt carries the fact.

Large food files are why the page feels late. [web.dev's Web Vitals guidance](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) treats Largest Contentful Paint as the loading measure, and a good experience means that paint happens within 2.5 seconds. A hero that is a print file will miss that on the sidewalk. Export for the size you display. Reserve the image's space so the button does not jump. Cumulative Layout Shift should stay at 0.1 or less. A caption that shoves the booking link is the photograph damaging the night.

### Selects a host would trust

Lay the selects on a table and read the captions to someone who takes reservations. They should be able to say which room, what the dish is, and whether the picture matches a night they would promise. If they say the room looks louder than it is, you shot the wrong hour. If they say the dish left the menu, change the frame or the caption before the page goes up.

Keep a small set per restaurant, not a dump from the last campaign. Street, room, one dish, one detail. Four frames can run for a season if they stay true. Add a frame when the menu's signature changes, and retire the frame that would make a guest order something you no longer cook. That retirement is part of direction. A site full of ghost dishes trains people to distrust the pictures.

Note the weight of the hero next to the select. If the file is heavy, export another. Direction includes the version the phone will actually show. A beautiful original that never arrives is not on the website, no matter how it looked in the edit. Hand the brief, the captions, and the crops to whoever publishes. A folder with no sentences will be published as a mood, because a mood is the easiest default.

Look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) when you want a reference for pictures that carry a specific subject instead of a general glow. Hanabi designs and builds marketing sites where the photograph and the sentence stay separate, so you can correct a dish name without reshooting. The standard is the same: one subject, one fact, no animation in the way.

## A frame for each door

Shoot the rooms as different places, even when they share a group. The guest is choosing a door. If every hero is the same candle and the same linen, the photographs have merged the restaurants you are trying to tell apart. Give each room one frame that would be false if you swapped the captions. A counter. A window onto a specific street. A dish that only that kitchen sends.

Keep the shared idea, if there is one, in a single quieter frame or in a sentence. The bakery that feeds three rooms can be a caption. It should not replace the three rooms. A guest who liked the loud bar should be able to see that the second site is a quiet lunch. The pictures have to allow that difference. If they do not, you will explain it forever at the host stand.

Retire a frame the week the room changes. New seats, a different dish, a lunch service that ended. Leaving the old photograph up is direction from a previous restaurant. The site will keep promising it. Put the new select in the same slot so the page structure stays and the truth moves.

Count the lead frames the way you count covers on a Saturday. One room, one dish, one street. If a restaurant has no street frame, the guest will not know the door. If it has no dish, they will not know the cooking. If it has five dishes and no room, they will not know if they can hear each other. Fill the gap with a shoot, not with a group-wide texture. A shared texture is how the second site becomes invisible. Name the photographer's job per room in the brief, so the day does not collapse into whatever room has the best light at 4 p.m. The best light is useless if it is always the same corner. Walk the rooms with the photographer before the camera comes out, and point at the seat you want a guest to imagine. That pointing is the direction. The rest is craft in service of it. When the contact sheet arrives, select against that point, not against which frame is sharpest. Sharp and wrong still sends the guest to the wrong night.

## The phone will recrop the plate

Desktop will flatter a wide room. The phone will cut it, or it will shrink the dish into a thumbnail. If the seat or the plate sits in the part of the frame you lose, the direction is unfinished. The next pass is the visit as a guest actually makes it.

That pass is [the mobile visit for a restaurant group](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-restaurant-group). Select as if that screen is the real one. For this guest, it is.
